Origins & "All Means All" Differentiation Philosophy

Developed under federal Jacob K. Javits grant funding by Dr. Sandra Kaplan, Bette Gould, and Sheila Madsen at the University of Southern California (USC), the Depth and Complexity Framework was engineered to replace quantitative acceleration ("give fast finishers more worksheets") with qualitative cognitive elevation.

In secondary mathematics, the framework shifts daily instruction away from passive formula memorization toward active reasoning modeled after professional mathematicians, statisticians, and quantitative analysts.

The "All Means All" Principle: Depth and Complexity prompts are universal access tools. Rather than pulling advanced students out of the room or creating isolated curriculum tracks, prompts allow teachers to differentiate heterogeneously within a single task—ensuring striving mathematicians, Multilingual Learners (MLs), and gifted students engage with identical core mathematical concepts at varying levels of cognitive demand.

Defining Dimensions in Secondary Math

Depth (Looking Inside): Investigating internal mathematical structures, underlying rules, domain restrictions, and non-obvious pattern behaviors within a single concept. Depth asks students to uncover how mathematical systems work internally (e.g., examining why division by zero disrupts algebraic structure or why function notation removes ambiguity in multi-variable equations).

Complexity (Looking Outward): Extending mathematical concepts outward across multiple representations (equations, tables, graphs, verbal models), over time, and through interdisciplinary applications. Complexity prompts students to relate mathematical concepts to broader contexts (e.g., connecting exponential functions to population decay models or physics velocity vectors).

The 4 Pillars of Framework Architecture

The framework consists of four integrated components that transform standard secondary math curriculum into high-cognitive-demand learning:

  • 11 Thinking Prompts: Visual lenses (8 Depth, 3 Complexity) that cue specific cognitive operations.
  • 5 Content Imperatives: Deepening dimensions (Origin, Contribution, Convergence, Parallel, Paradox) that challenge advanced mathematical reasoning.
  • Universal Concepts & Generalizations: Broad themes (Systems, Relationships, Change, Order) that unify isolated math topics across grade levels.
  • Disciplinarian Thinking: Prompting students to analyze problems using the professional tools, habits, and vocabulary of authentic domain experts (statisticians, actuaries, engineers).

Secondary Math HQIM Problem Types & Cognitive Alignment

High-Quality Instructional Materials (HQIM) incorporate specialized problem structures designed to trigger depth and complexity reasoning without requiring separate lesson plans:

  • Worked Examples (Rules ): Students analyze complete solution paths to critique reasoning, isolate governing algebraic properties, and explain step-by-step logic.
  • Thumbs Up / Thumbs Down (Ethics ): Students evaluate competing solution paths, spot misconceptions (e.g., sign errors in distribution), and justify the mathematically sound path.
  • Who's Correct? (Multiple Perspectives ): Students compare multiple valid solution methods (algebraic, tabular, graphical) to evaluate efficiency and identify boundary constraints.
  • Thought Bubbles & Getting Started (Patterns ): Exploratory prompts that lead students to detect recurring structural patterns and form mathematical conjectures.

Module 2: Question Laddering & Byrdseed Mathematical Inquiry

🔊 Audio Assist:

Attaching an icon to a basic recall problem creates zero cognitive growth. To generate true rigor, educators build Question Ladders—sequencing prompts from low-floor recall up to evaluative synthesis using the Byrdseed 4-Step Model.

Exemplar Byrdseed 4-Step Question Ladder (Secondary Math):
• Step 1 (Low Floor - Patterns ): What recurring pattern of change do you observe in the function's output table?
• Step 2 (Analysis - Rules ): Compare the algebraic rules governing linear constant differences vs. exponential constant multipliers in these data sets.
• Step 3 (Evaluation - Unanswered Questions / Ethics ): Critique which mathematical representation best reveals extraneous solutions or domain constraints.
• Step 4 (High Ceiling - Across Disciplines ): Reformulate the contextual problem using formal function notation f(x) and translate the growth behavior into an economic inflation model.

Embedded Secondary Math Sources for Laddering Task

Click each tab below to view and study the document directly on screen:

Source Document: Grade 6 - Bar None (One-Step Addition Equations)

Students use bar models to solve one-step addition equations, decompose expressions, isolate variables with inverse operations, and apply the Subtraction Property of Equality.

Source Document: Grade 7 - Right Triangle Connection (Pythagorean Theorem)

Students explore geometric area proofs of the Pythagorean Theorem (a² + b² = c²), proving leg square sum equalities and solving real-world context problems.

Source Document: Algebra 1 - Uptown and Downtown (Exponential Growth & Decay)

Students compare simple interest vs. exponential compound growth, sort function representations, graph decay models, and analyze asymptotic end behaviors.

Module 3: The 11 Thinking Prompts — Official Kaplan Interactive Suite

🔊 Audio Assist:

Click on each 3D card below to flip it and study its mathematical definition, high-leverage question stems, and secondary math applications using the official Depth & Complexity icon set. You must flip all 11 cards to unlock the Identify the Icon activity and the reflection canvas.

Language of the Discipline
Focus: Specialized vocabulary, mathematical symbols, and formal notation.

Secondary Math Example: Utilizing function notation f(x), domain, range, asymptote, vertex, and coefficient terms.
Details
Focus: Defining attributes, variables, components, and key coordinates.

Secondary Math Example: Isolating vertex coordinates (h, k), axis of symmetry, x-intercepts, and initial boundary parameters.
Ethics
Focus: Statistical bias, manipulative scale choices, dilemmas, and values.

Secondary Math Example: Evaluating truncated graph axes in news media or calculating predatory compound interest models.
Unanswered Questions
Focus: Ambiguities, unknown variables, edge cases, and undefined values.

Secondary Math Example: Investigating extraneous solutions in radical equations or point discontinuities in rational functions.
Over Time
Focus: Temporal shifts, historical evolution, past/present/future comparisons.

Secondary Math Example: Tracing function output behavior over time or historical development of proof systems.
Across Disciplines
Focus: Real-world modeling, interdisciplinary links, and cross-curricular application.

Secondary Math Example: Linking linear regression to economic rent models or quadratics to physics trajectories.
Trends
Focus: External drivers, rate-of-change shifts, directions, and trajectories.

Secondary Math Example: Analyzing polynomial end behaviors as x approaches infinity and interval growth trends.
Patterns
Focus: Recurring sequences, growth cycles, symmetry, and predictability.

Secondary Math Example: Distinguishing linear constant differences from exponential constant multiplicative growth.
Big Idea
Focus: Overarching theorems, global generalizations, and core principles.

Secondary Math Example: Proving the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra or formalizing function mapping uniqueness.
Rules
Focus: Governing laws, properties of equality, structure, and constraints.

Secondary Math Example: Enforcing domain restrictions (x ≠ 0, non-negative radicands) and applying the Vertical Line Test.
Multiple Perspectives
Focus: Diverse solution paths, viewpoints, and alternative strategies.

Secondary Math Example: Comparing substitution, elimination, and graphing methods for linear systems.

Module 4: Secondary Math Task Auditing & Differentiation Equation

🔊 Audio Assist:

Dr. Sandra Kaplan’s Differentiation Equation provides a structured mechanics formula for adapting standard grade-level secondary math curriculum objectives into high-demand tasks:

Differentiated Secondary Math Objective Example:
Standard Objective: "Solve quadratic equations using the quadratic formula."
Differentiated Formulation: Students will critique (T/S) quadratic functions (C) by analyzing the convergence (Content Imperative) of rate-of-change trends (Depth) and graphical vs. algebraic perspectives (Complexity) to isolate domain rules , using dynamic graphing applets (R/S), to construct a comparative error-analysis report (P).

Task Audit: 5-Set Secondary Math Rigor Review

Review the 5 secondary math task pairs below. Click on the option in each set that successfully elevates cognitive demand using official Depth & Complexity icons.

Set 1 - Option A

Find the roots of y = x² - 4 using the quadratic formula and check your answer on a calculator.

Set 1 - Option B

Critique quadratic functions by analyzing rate-of-change trends and graphical vs. algebraic perspectives to identify domain rules .

Set 2 - Option A

Compare substitution, elimination, and graphical intersection perspectives for a linear system to evaluate which method highlights edge cases .

Set 2 - Option B

Solve 10 systems of equations problems using substitution and box your final coordinate answers.

Set 3 - Option A

Calculate the mean, median, and mode for a given list of 15 test scores.

Set 3 - Option B

Analyze statistical graphs in media. Evaluate how truncated y-axis scales violate ethical standards and alter public interpretation trends .

Set 4 - Option A

Distinguish linear constant differences from exponential multiplicative growth patterns to enforce domain restrictions .

Set 4 - Option B

Plug x = 3 into the function f(x) = 2^x and evaluate the numerical result.

Set 5 - Option A

Memorize the definitions of SSS, SAS, and ASA triangle congruence postulates for tomorrow's quiz.

Set 5 - Option B

Trace the axiomatic origins of geometric proofs and compare paragraph vs. two-column proof perspectives .
